section.heading: 7.5. Volumes of Solids of Revolution
Finding the Volume of a Solid of Revolution
section.paragraph: In this section we use a Riemann sum to find a formula for computing the volume of a solid that results when a region is revolved about an axis. The solid is called a solid of revolution . To find the volume of a solid of revolution, suppose the plane region under the curve defined by a nonnegative continuous function $$y = f(x)$$ between $$x = a$$ and $$x = b$$ is revolved about the $$x$$ -axis (Figure 16).

image.alt: Details Two graphs a and b depict a curve between an interval and the solid swept by the region under the curve in same interval respectively. In the graph a, labeled Region R under the curve shows a curve, a curve is graphed in the x y coordinate plane. The horizontal axis x has two tick marks labeled a and b. The curve begins a short distance above the x axis, rises upward to the right, concave up, till it reaches near the top right corner of the viewing window. A perpendicular each is dropped from the beginning and end of the curve. The region under the curve between the perpendiculars is shaded and labeled R. A rotational arrow on the positive x axis indicates that this area is rotated counterclockwise about the x axis. In the graph B, a solid, labeled S, resembling a loudspeaker is graphed. The solid has been obtained by shading the region the curve in graph a has swept as it was rotated about the x axis.

section.paragraph: To derive a formula for finding the volume of the solid of revolution, we divide the interval $$\left\lbrack {a,b} \right\rbrack$$ into $$n$$ subintervals, each of equal length, by means of the points $$x_{0} = a,x_{1},x_{2},\ldots,x_{n} = b$$ , so that the length of each subinterval is given by $$\Delta x = {\left( {b - a} \right) \slash n}$$ . Also, let $$p_{1},p_{2},\ldots,p_{n}$$ be points in the subintervals $$\left\lbrack {x_{0},x_{1}} \right\rbrack,\left\lbrack {x_{1},x_{2}} \right\rbrack,\ldots,\left\lbrack {x_{n - 1},x_{n}} \right\rbrack$$ , respectively (Figure 17).

image.alt: Details A curve is graphed in the x y coordinate plane. The horizontal axis x, has tick marks a = x_0, x_1, x_i minus 1, x_i, x_n minus 1, x_n = b from left to right at unequal intervals. The vertical axis y has 3 tick marks at unequal intervals labeled f(p_1), f(p_i), and f(p_n). From each of these tick marks in the vertical axis, a horizontal line runs parallel to the x axis and meets the curve and from each of these meeting points represented as a closed circle, a perpendicular is dropped to the x axis meeting it at p_1, p_i, and p_n respectively. The curve labeled y = f(x) starts in the first quadrant little away from the origin, concave up, increasing to the right passing through the closed circles and exits the first quadrant through the coordinate (p_n, f (p_n) at the top right corner of the viewing window. 6 perpendiculars are raised from the tick marks, x_0, x_1, x_i minus 1, x_i, x_n minus 1, x_n to meet the path of the curve forming 3 trapezoids. The region between the curve and the x axis, bounded by the perpendiculars from x_i minus 1, and x_i is shaded and labeled R.

figure.caption: The region $$R$$ is revolved about the $$x$$ -axis.

section.paragraph: Let’s concentrate on the part of the solid of revolution that is swept out by revolving the region under the curve between $$x = x_{i - 1}$$ and $$x = x_{i}$$ about the $$x$$ -axis. The volume $$\Delta V_{i}$$ of this object, shown in Figure 18a, may be approximated by the volume of the disk shown in Figure 18b, of radius $$f\left( p_{i} \right)$$ and width $$\Delta x$$ , obtained by revolving the rectangular region of height $$f\left( p_{i} \right)$$ and width $$\Delta x$$ about the $$x$$ -axis (Figure 18c).

The region below the curve till the central horizontal line is shaded. The horizontal line that grazed the top of the disc meets the curve at approximately its midpoint labeled (p_i, f (p_i)). The height of this point from the central horizontal line is labeled f(p_i). The horizontal width of the shaded region is labeled delta x.

This analysis suggests that the volume of the solid of revolution may be approximated by the sum of the volumes of $$n$$ suitable disks—namely,

$$\pi\left\lbrack {f\left( p_{1} \right)} \right\rbrack^{2}\Delta x + \pi\left\lbrack {f\left( p_{2} \right)} \right\rbrack^{2}\Delta x + \cdots + \pi\left\lbrack {f\left( p_{n} \right)} \right\rbrack^{2}\Delta x$$

(shown in Figure 19). This last expression is a Riemann sum of the function $$g(x) = \pi\left\lbrack {f(x)} \right\rbrack^{2}$$ over the interval $$\left\lbrack {a,b} \right\rbrack$$ . Letting $$n$$ approach infinity, we obtain Formula 18.

example.heading: Example 1
example.paragraph: Find the volume of the solid of revolution obtained by revolving the region under the curve $$y = f(x) = \sqrt{x}$$ from $$x = 0$$ to $$x = 2$$ about the $$x$$ -axis.
example.heading: Solution
example.paragraph: The region under the curve and the resulting solid of revolution are shown in Figure 20.

image.alt: Details Two graphs a and b depict a curve at an interval 0 to 2 and the solid swept by the region under the curve in same interval respectively. In graph a, labeled the region under the curve y = sqrt(x) from x = 0 to x = 2, a curve is graphed in the x y coordinate plane. The horizontal axis x, ranges from 0 to over 2 and the vertical axis y is unlabeled. The curve enters the first quadrant through the origin, concave down, increasing to the right, to reach a point at the top right in the first quadrant from where a perpendicular is dropped to the x axis to meet the x coordinate x = 2. The region between the curve and the x axis, bounded by the perpendicular is shaded and labeled R. A vertical rectangular region with horizontal width delta x and vertical height y is highlighted in the region R. In graph B, the solid of revolution obtained when R is revolved about the x-axis, labeled S in the x y coordinate plane, resembles a cone with curved apex and sides, opening rightward with its vertex is at the origin and symmetric about the positive x axis. A disc shaped solid is highlighted withing the cone indicating the region swept by the shaded rectangle from graph a.

figure.caption: If $$R$$ is revolved about the $$x$$ -axis, we obtain the solid of revolution $$S$$ .

example.paragraph: Using Formula (18), we find that the required volume is given by

$$\begin{array}{l} {{\pi{\int_{0}^{2}{\left( \sqrt{x} \right)^{2}dx}}}{= \pi{\int_{0}^{2}{xdx}}}} \\ {\phantom{\pi{\int_{0}^{2}{\left( \sqrt{x} \right)^{2}dx}}}{= \left. \frac{\pi}{2}x^{2} \right|_{0}^{2} = \frac{\pi}{2}\left( {4 - 0} \right) = 2\pi}} \end{array}$$

example.heading: Example 2
example.paragraph: Derive a formula for the volume of a right circular cone of radius $$r$$ and height $$h$$ .
example.heading: Solution
example.paragraph: The cone is shown in Figure 21a. It is the solid of revolution obtained by revolving the region $$R$$ of Figure 21b about the $$x$$ -axis. The region $$R$$ is the region under the straight line $$y = f(x) = \left( {r \slash h} \right)x$$ between $$x = 0$$ and $$x = h$$ .

image.alt: Details Two graphs a and b depict a solid swept by the region under a curve and the curve respectively. The graph A, labeled a right circular cone of radius r and height h shows an inverted cone with radius r and vertical height h. In graph B, labeled R is the region under the straight line y = (r/h) x from x = 0 to x = h, a straight line enters from the third quadrant, passes through the origin and rises upward to the right into the first quadrant. From a point on the line, labeled (h, r), a perpendicular is dropped to the x axis meeting it at (h, 0). The height of the perpendicular is labeled r. The region bound by the line, the perpendicular and the x axis is shaded and labeled R. A rotational arrow indicates the shaded region is rotated about the x axis.

example.paragraph: Using Formula (18), we see that the required volume is given by

$$\begin{array}{l} {V{= \pi{\int_{0}^{h}{\left\lbrack {\left( \frac{r}{h} \right)x} \right\rbrack^{2}dx = \frac{\pi r^{2}}{h^{2}}{\int_{0}^{h}{x^{2}dx}}}}}} \\ {\phantom{V}{\left. = \left( \frac{\pi r^{2}}{3h^{2}} \right)x^{3} \right|_{0}^{h} = \frac{1}{3}\pi r^{2}h}} \end{array}$$

example.heading: Example 3
example.paragraph: Find the volume of the solid of revolution obtained by revolving the region bounded by the curves $$y = e^{x}$$ and $$y = x^{2} + \frac{1}{2}$$ from $$x = 0$$ to $$x = 1$$ about the $$x$$ -axis (Figure 23).

image.alt: Details Two curves are graphed in the x y coordinate plane. The horizontal axis x ranges from 0 to over 1 and the vertical axis y ranges from 0 to over 3. The first curve labeled y = e^x enters the first quadrant around (0, 1), slopes upward to the right, concave up increasing steeply to the right and exits the first quadrant at the top right of the viewing window. The second curve labeled y = x^2 + (1/2), which slopes completely below the first curve enters the first quadrant around (0, 0.6), slopes upward to the right, concave up increasing gradually to the right away from the first curve and exits the first quadrant. A perpendicular is raised from the coordinate (1, 0), which cuts both the curves. The region between the two curves enclosed by the perpendicular is shaded and labeled R.

figure.caption: $$R$$ is the region bounded by the curves $$y = e^{x}$$ and $$y = x^{2} + \frac{1}{2}$$ from $$x = 0$$ to $$x = 1$$ .

example.heading: Solution
example.paragraph: Using Formula (19) with $$f(x) = e^{x}$$ and $$g(x) = x^{2} + \frac{1}{2}$$ , we see that the required volume is given by

$$\begin{array}{l} {V{= \pi{\int_{0}^{1}{\left\lbrack {\left( e^{x} \right)^{2} - \left( {x^{2} + \frac{1}{2}} \right)^{2}} \right\rbrack dx}}}} \\ {\phantom{V}{= \pi{\int_{0}^{1}{\left( {e^{2x} - x^{4} - x^{2} - \frac{1}{4}} \right)dx}}}} \\ {\phantom{V}{= \left. \pi\left( {\frac{1}{2}e^{2x} - \frac{1}{5}x^{5} - \frac{1}{3}x^{3} - \frac{1}{4}x} \right) \right|_{0}^{1}}} \\ {\phantom{V}{= \pi\left\lbrack {\left( {\frac{1}{2}e^{2} - \frac{1}{5} - \frac{1}{3} - \frac{1}{4}} \right) - \frac{1}{2}} \right\rbrack}} \\ {\phantom{V}{= \frac{\pi}{60}\left( {30e^{2} - 77} \right)}} \end{array}$$
or approximately $$7.57$$ .

example.heading: Example 4
example.paragraph: Find the volume of the solid obtained by revolving the region bounded by the curves $$y = f(x) = x^{2}$$ and $$y = g(x) = x^{3}$$ about the $$x$$ -axis.
example.heading: Solution
example.paragraph: We first find the point(s) of intersection of the two curves by solving the system of equations
$$\left\{ \begin{array}{l} {y = x^{2}} \\ {y = x^{3}} \end{array} \right.$$
We have

The first curve labeled y = g(x) = x^3 enters the third quadrant at the bottom left of the viewing window, slopes upward to reach the horizontal axis, continues to slope along the horizontal axis, reaches the origin, enters the first quadrant, concave up, increasing to the right and exits the first quadrant at the top right corner of the viewing window. The second curve labeled y = f(x) = x^2enters from the second, slopes downward, cuts the vertical axis at the origin to enter the first quadrant, concave up, increasing to the right below and away the first curve, then slopes closer and cuts the first curve around (1, 1) to exit the first quadrant at the top right corner of the viewing window above the first curve. example.paragraph: Next, observe that $$g(x) \leq f(x)$$ for all values of $$x$$ between $$x = 0$$ and $$x = 1$$ , so using Formula (19), we find the required volume to be

$$\begin{array}{l} {V{= \pi{\int_{0}^{1}{\lbrack{{(x^{2})}^{2} - {(x^{3})}^{2}}\rbrack}}dx}} \\ {\phantom{V}{= \pi{\int_{0}^{1}{({x^{4} - x^{6}})dx}}}} \\ {\phantom{V}{= \pi{\left( {\frac{1}{5}x^{5} - \frac{1}{7}x^{7}} \right)\left. \right|}_{0}^{1}}} \\ {\phantom{V}{= \pi\left( {\frac{1}{5} - \frac{1}{7}} \right)}} \\ {\phantom{V}{= \frac{2\pi}{35}}} \end{array}$$

section.heading: 7.5. Concept Questions

list.item: If $$f$$ is a nonnegative function on the interval $$\left\lbrack {a,b} \right\rbrack$$ and the region under the graph of $$f$$ from $$x = a$$ to $$x = b$$ is revolved about the $$x$$ -axis, what is the volume of the resulting solid of revolution?
